claim: ADAM17 is a membrane-tethered metalloprotease that is the primary shedding enzyme responsible for the release of the inflammatory cytokine TNFα.
source: ADAM17, a membrane-tethered metalloprotease, is the primary shedding enzyme responsible for the release of the inflammatory cytokine TNFα and several EGF receptor ligands.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Black et al., 1997; Moss et al., 1997).

claim: ADAM17 is the primary shedding enzyme responsible for the release of several EGF receptor ligands.
source: ADAM17, a membrane-tethered metalloprotease, is the primary shedding enzyme responsible for the release of the inflammatory cytokine TNFα and several EGF receptor ligands.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Sahin et al., 2004; Sahin and Blobel, 2007).

claim: iRhom proteins act as cofactors that regulate ADAM17 substrate shedding.
source: ADAM17 exists in complex with the rhomboid-like iRhom proteins, which act as cofactors that regulate ADAM17 substrate shedding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous work cited in the introduction (Grieve et al., 2017).

claim: FRMD8 is a new component of the iRhom2/ADAM17 sheddase complex.
source: Here we report that the poorly characterised FERM domain-containing protein FRMD8 is a new component of the iRhom2/ADAM17 sheddase complex.
evidence: This is the main finding reported in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1.

claim: FRMD8 binds to the cytoplasmic N-terminus of iRhoms.
source: FRMD8 binds to the cytoplasmic N-terminus of iRhoms and is necessary to stabilise iRhoms and ADAM17 at the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by deletion mapping experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: FRMD8 is necessary to stabilise iRhoms and ADAM17 at the cell surface.
source: FRMD8 binds to the cytoplasmic N-terminus of iRhoms and is necessary to stabilise iRhoms and ADAM17 at the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing reduced cell surface levels of iRhom2 and ADAM17 in FRMD8 knockout cells (Figures 2D, 7A).

claim: In the absence of FRMD8, iRhom2 and ADAM17 are degraded via the endolysosomal pathway.
source: In the absence of FRMD8, iRhom2 and ADAM17 are degraded via the endolysosomal pathway, resulting in the reduction of ADAM17-mediated shedding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunofluorescence data showing colocalization with LAMP1 (Figure 6) and rescue by lysosomal inhibitors (Figure 6G).

claim: Loss of FRMD8 results in the reduction of ADAM17-mediated shedding.
source: In the absence of FRMD8, iRhom2 and ADAM17 are degraded via the endolysosomal pathway, resulting in the reduction of ADAM17-mediated shedding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by shedding assays showing reduced release of AREG, HB-EGF, and TGFα in FRMD8 knockout cells (Figure 2E, F).

claim: FRMD8 knockout iPSC-derived human macrophages show reduced TNFα release in response to LPS stimulation.
source: Consistent with our biochemical data, these mutant macrophages were defective in their ability to release TNFα in response to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulation, demonstrating the pathophysiological importance of FRMD8 in the normal inflammatory response by human macrophages.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ELISA data from iPSC-derived macrophages (Figure 9C).

claim: FRMD8 was identified as the top hit in a mass spectrometry screen for iRhom2 binding partners.
source: The top hit by a long way, however, was FRMD8 (Figure 1A, Table 1), a poorly studied protein that has not previously been implicated in iRhom function, ADAM17 regulation, and growth factor or cytokine signalling.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the volcano plot in Figure 1A and quantitative data in Table 1.

claim: ADAM17 was detected as a statistically significant hit in the iRhom2 co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry screen.
source: Validating the overall approach, we detected ADAM17, the known iRhom2 interacting protein (Adrain et al., 2012; McIlwain et al., 2012; Christova et al., 2013) as a statistically significant hit (Figure 1A, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data in Figure 1A and Table 1.

claim: Several 14-3-3 proteins and MAPK1/3 were detected as hits in the iRhom2 co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry screen.
source: Among the hits were several 14-3-3 proteins (eta, epsilon, gamma, sigma, theta, zeta/delta) and MAPK1/3 (Table 1), which we have previously reported to participate in the regulation of inflammatory signalling by phosphorylation of iRhom2 (Grieve et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the mass spectrometry data in Table 1 and previous work (Grieve et al., 2017).

claim: FRMD8-V5 co-immunoprecipitates with iRhom1-3xHA and iRhom2-3xHA.
source: C-terminally V5-tagged FRMD8 co-immunoprecipitated with either iRhom1-3xHA or iRhom2-3xHA (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: iRhom1-3xHA and iRhom2-3xHA can be pulled down with an antibody against the V5 tag when co-expressed with FRMD8-V5.
source: Conversely, we pulled down both iRhom1-3xHA and iRhom2-3xHA with an antibody against the V5 tag.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Endogenous FRMD8 co-immunoprecipitates with iRhom2-3xHA.
source: Finally, we were also able to co-immunoprecipitate endogenous FRMD8 with iRhom2-3xHA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FRMD8 is a FERM domain-containing protein predicted to be a soluble cytoplasmic protein.
source: As its name indicates, FRMD8 is a FERM (4.1/ezrin/radixin/moesin) domain-containing protein. It is predicted to be a soluble cytoplasmic protein, and the only report about its function describes it as binding to the Wnt accessory receptor low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 6 (LRP6), and negatively regulating Wnt signalling (Kategaya et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the protein name and previous literature (Kategaya et al., 2009).

claim: Loss of FRMD8 by siRNA or CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene deletion drastically reduces mature ADAM17 protein levels in HEK293T cells.
source: In both cases, loss of FRMD8 drastically reduced the protein levels of mature ADAM17 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Loss of FRMD8 does not affect ADAM10 maturation.
source: This effect was specific to ADAM17, as the maturation of its closest homologue, ADAM10, was unaffected by loss of FRMD8 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of FRMD8-V5 rescues mature ADAM17 levels in FRMD8 knockout HEK293T cells.
source: Moreover, mature ADAM17 levels were rescued by expression of FRMD8-V5 in FRMD8 knockout HEK293T cells (Figure 2C), confirming that the phenotype was caused by FRMD8 loss.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Loss of FRMD8 results in reduced cell surface levels of ADAM17 but not ADAM10.
source: Finally, in addition to this reduction of mature ADAM17 caused by FRMD8 loss, we found a striking loss of ADAM17, but not ADAM10, on the cell surface (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: PMA-stimulated shedding of AP-tagged AREG and HB-EGF is substantially reduced in FRMD8 knockout cells.
source: The shedding of alkaline phosphatase (AP)-tagged EGF receptor ligands AREG and HB-EGF, after stimulation with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA), were both substantially reduced in FRMD8 knockout cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by shedding assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Both PMA-stimulated and constitutive shedding of AP-tagged TGFα are significantly reduced in FRMD8 knockout cells.
source: Again, FRMD8 knockout cells released significantly less AP-TGFα compared to wild-type cells, both after stimulation but also after 20 hr of constitutive shedding (Figure 2F), implying that mutant cells had fundamental defects in their ability to shed ADAM17 ligands, regardless of PMA stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by shedding assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The FRMD8 binding site on iRhom2 lies within amino acids 201-300 of the N-terminus.
source: Deletion of the first 200 amino acids in the N-terminus of iRhom2 (iRhom2∆200) did not disrupt FRMD8 binding, but no interaction was detected in mutants greater than ∆300 (Figure 3B), implying that the region between 200 and 300 amino acids was necessary for FRMD8 binding. An internal deletion of amino acids 201–300 within iRhom2 (iRhom2∆201-300) led to the loss of exogenous FRMD8 binding (Figure 3C), confirming that the FRMD8 binding site lies within this region.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with deletion mutants shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: iRhom1/2 DKO cells reconstituted with iRhom2∆201-300 show reduced ADAM17-mediated shedding of AREG.
source: In line with this, an iRhom1/2 DKO cell line reconstituted with iRhom2∆201-300 showed a similar deficiency to FRMD8 KO cells in ADAM17-mediated shedding of AREG (compare Figures 3D and 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by shedding assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: iRhom1/2 DKO cells reconstituted with iRhom2∆201-300 show reduced levels of mature ADAM17.
source: This reduction in shedding correlates with a reduction in the level of mature ADAM17 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The mouse iRhom2 curly-bare (cub) mutant lacks the FRMD8 binding site.
source: Interestingly, the FRMD8 binding site is also absent in a mouse iRhom2 mutant called curly-bare (cub), which lacks residues 1–268 (Hosur et al., 2014; Siggs et al., 2014). Sequence alignment shows that the deletion of 268 amino acids in mouse iRhom2 corresponds to the loss of residues 1–298 in the human protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and previous literature (Hosur et al., 2014; Siggs et al., 2014).

claim: Full-length mouse iRhom2 binds human FRMD8, but the cub mutant cannot.
source: Consistent with this mapping data, we found that whereas full-length mouse iRhom2 bound human FRMD8, the cub mutant cannot (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FRMD8 co-immunoprecipitates with both immature and mature ADAM17 as well as iRhom2.
source: When performing an immunoprecipitation of FRMD8, we found both immature and mature ADAM17 as well as iRhom2 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: FRMD8 and iRhom2 co-immunoprecipitate in ADAM17 knockout cells.
source: We found that exogenous FRMD8 and iRhom2 co-immunoprecipitated with each other in ADAM17 knockout cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: iRhom2 and ADAM17 can interact with each other in FRMD8 knockout cells.
source: In turn, iRhom2 and ADAM17 were still able to interact with each other in FRMD8 knockout cells (Figure 4C), showing that FRMD8 is not essential for the iRhom/ADAM17 sheddase complex to form.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FRMD8 does not pull down ADAM17 in cells mutant for both iRhoms.
source: In contrast, FRMD8 did not pull down ADAM17 in cells mutant for both iRhoms (Figure 4D). This demonstrated that there is no direct link between FRMD8 and ADAM17; instead both bind simultaneously to iRhom2.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: FRMD8 co-immunoprecipitates with pro- or mature ADAM17 in iRhom1/2 DKO cells reconstituted with iRhom2WT, but not with iRhom2∆201-300.
source: Supporting this, FRMD8 co-immunoprecipitated with pro- or mature ADAM17 in iRhom1/2 DKO cells reconstituted with iRhom2WT, but not with iRhom2∆201-300 (Figure 4D), the mutant that does not bind to FRMD8 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: FRMD8 binds to both iRhom2/proADAM17 and iRhom2/mature ADAM17 complexes but associates preferentially with iRhom2/mature ADAM17 complexes.
source: FRMD8 binds to both iRhom2/proADAM17 and iRhom2/mature ADAM17 complexes but associates preferentially with iRhom2/mature ADAM17 complexes (Figure 4A,D), which have been shown to exist at the cell surface (Grieve et al., 2017; Cavadas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A and 4D, and previous literature (Grieve et al., 2017; Cavadas et al., 2017).

claim: Overexpression of FRMD8-V5 in iRhom1/2 DKO cells reconstituted with wild-type iRhom2 leads to increased plasma membrane localization of iRhom2.
source: Overexpression of FRMD8-V5 in iRhom1/2 DKO cells reconstituted with wild-type iRhom2 led to a striking increase in plasma membrane iRhom2 (Figure 5A), which in wild-type cells is almost exclusively observed within the endoplasmic reticulum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The iRhom2∆300 mutant does not undergo ER-to-plasma membrane relocalisation upon FRMD8 overexpression.
source: As a control, the iRhom2∆300 mutant, which cannot bind to FRMD8 (Figure 3B), did not undergo the same ER-to-plasma membrane relocalisation upon FRMD8 overexpression.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The iRhom2 N-terminus is required for FRMD8 localisation at the cell surface.
source: Indicating a reciprocal relationship between the two proteins, we also observed that the iRhom2 N-terminus was required for FRMD8 localisation at the cell surface (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Fusion of FRMD8 to the N-terminus of iRhom2∆300 shifts its localization from the ER to the plasma membrane.
source: Strikingly, we saw that the normal ER localisation of iRhom2∆300 (Figure 5D) shifted to the plasma membrane upon fusion to FRMD8 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: The localization of ADAM17-V5 follows that of iRhom in both iRhom2∆300 and FRMD8-iRhom2∆300 cells.
source: Furthermore, we found that the localisation of ADAM17-V5 followed that of iRhom in both conditions: in iRhom2∆300 cells ADAM17 localised to the ER, and in FRMD8-iRhom2∆300 cells it was readily observed at the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: FRMD8-iRhom2∆300 shows higher total levels of iRhom2 compared to iRhom2∆300.
source: We also noted that FRMD8-iRhom2∆300 showed strikingly higher total levels of iRhom2 (Figure 5E), which hinted that FRMD8 may play a role in the protein turnover of iRhoms at the cell surface.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: FRMD8-iRhom2∆300 is much more stable compared to iRhom2∆300 or iRhom2WT in cycloheximide chase experiments.
source: In line with these observations, we found that FRMD8-iRhom2∆300 was much more stable compared to iRhom2∆300 or iRhom2WT as seen in cells incubated with cycloheximide (CHX) to block the synthesis of new proteins (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 5F (which appears to be referenced as Figure 7—figure supplement 1A based on the figure legends).

claim: Upon treatment with bafilomycin A1, both iRhom2WT and iRhom2∆300 accumulate in LAMP1-positive lysosomal puncta.
source: However, upon treatment with the lysosomal degradation inhibitor, bafilomycin A1, both proteins accumulated in LAMP1-positive lysosomal puncta (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: iRhom2∆300 overlaps completely with LAMP1 after bafilomycin treatment, while iRhom2WT shows only partial colocalization.
source: Interestingly, unlike the partial colocalisation between LAMP1 and iRhom2WT (Figure 6C), iRhom2∆300 overlapped completely with LAMP1 (indicated by the arrows in Figure 6D). This confirmed that in the absence of FRMD8 recruitment, iRhom2 is constitutively sent to lysosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: The lysosomal pool of iRhom2∆300 colocalizes with ADAM17-V5 after bafilomycin treatment.
source: Importantly, this lysosomal pool of iRhom2∆300 also colocalised with ADAM17-V5 after bafilomycin treatment (highlighted with arrows in Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: After 16 hr of treatment with lysosomal degradation inhibitors bafilomycin and ammonium chloride, the mature form of ADAM17 is partially restored in FRMD8 knockout cells.
source: After 16 hr of treatment with the lysosomal degradation inhibitors bafilomycin and ammonium chloride, the mature form of ADAM17 was partially restored (Figure 6G; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The proteasomal inhibitor MG132 has no effect on the stability of mature ADAM17 in FRMD8 knockout cells.
source: In line with this interpretation, the proteasomal inhibitor MG132 had no effect on the stability of mature ADAM17 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A (which appears to be referenced as Figure 6G based on the figure legends).

claim: In the absence of FRMD8, there is a significant loss of cell surface iRhom2.
source: In the absence of FRMD8 we detected a significant loss of cell surface iRhom2 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A reduction of total iRhom2 levels is not detectable in FRMD8 knockout cells.
source: In line with our observation that cell surface iRhom2 represents only a small fraction of the total pool, a reduction of total iRhom2 levels was not detectable (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: There are no defects in the ER-based iRhom2/proADAM17 interaction in FRMD8 knockout cells.
source: Consistent with our conclusion that FRMD8 primarily functions late in the iRhom2/ADAM17 relationship, we detected no defects in the ER-based iRhom2/proADAM17 interaction in FRMD8 knockout cells (Figure 4C), nor in the trafficking of iRhom2 from the ER to the Golgi (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C and deglycosylation assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There are no defects in the trafficking of iRhom2 from the ER to the Golgi in FRMD8 knockout cells.
source: Consistent with our conclusion that FRMD8 primarily functions late in the iRhom2/ADAM17 relationship, we detected no defects in the ER-based iRhom2/proADAM17 interaction in FRMD8 knockout cells (Figure 4C), nor in the trafficking of iRhom2 from the ER to the Golgi (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by deglycosylation assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Overexpression of FRMD8 leads to increased levels of tagged iRhom2 and iRhom1.
source: A more direct demonstration of this stabilising function is provided by overexpressing FRMD8, which leads to increased levels of tagged iRhom2 (Figure 7C), as well as iRhom1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The 50 kDa N-terminally truncated fragment of iRhoms is not stabilised by FRMD8 expression.
source: Note that the 50 kDa N-terminally truncated fragment of iRhoms detected in western blots (Nakagawa et al., 2005; Adrain et al., 2012; Maney et al., 2015) is not stabilised by FRMD8 expression (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D, and previous literature (Nakagawa et al., 2005; Adrain et al., 2012; Maney et al., 2015).

claim: Overexpression of iRhom2 leads to the stabilisation of endogenous FRMD8 protein without affecting FRMD8 mRNA levels.
source: Intriguingly, the stabilisation of iRhom2 and FRMD8 is mutual: overexpression of iRhom2 consistently led to the stabilisation of endogenous FRMD8 protein (Figure 7D) without affecting FRMD8 mRNA levels (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7D and qPCR data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: FRMD8 overexpression leads to an increase in endogenous iRhom2 levels in cells with endogenously tagged iRhom2.
source: In these cells FRMD8 overexpression led to an increase in endogenous iRhom2 levels (Figure 8A); conversely, siRNA knockdown of FRMD8 caused a reduction of iRhom2 protein (Figure 8B), but no change of iRhom2 mRNA levels (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: siRNA knockdown of FRMD8 causes a reduction of endogenous iRhom2 protein but no change of iRhom2 mRNA levels.
source: In these cells FRMD8 overexpression led to an increase in endogenous iRhom2 levels (Figure 8A); conversely, siRNA knockdown of FRMD8 caused a reduction of iRhom2 protein (Figure 8B), but no change of iRhom2 mRNA levels (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8B and qPCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The 50 kDa iRhom2 fragment is not affected by FRMD8 levels in cells with endogenously tagged iRhom2.
source: Again, the 50 kDa iRhom2 fragment was not affected by FRMD8 levels (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: The 50 kDa iRhom fragment exists endogenously.
source: Parenthetically, this is the first reported evidence that this iRhom fragment exists endogenously, although its functional significance remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data from endogenously tagged iRhom2 cells shown in Figure 8A and 8B.

claim: FRMD8 knockout iPSC-derived macrophages express no detectable FRMD8 and show severely reduced levels of mature ADAM17.
source: These mutant macrophages expressed no detectable FRMD8 and, as in the HEK293T cells, showed severely reduced levels of mature ADAM17 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: TNFα shedding from FRMD8 knockout iPSC-derived macrophages is reduced when challenged with LPS.
source: When challenged with the inflammatory trigger LPS, TNFα shedding from the cells, as measured by ELISA, was reduced (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The ADAM10 inhibitor GI254023X has no effect on TNFα release from iPSC-derived macrophages, whereas the ADAM10/17 inhibitor GW further reduces TNFα release.
source: Confirming the expected specificity, the ADAM10 inhibitor GI254023X (GI) had no effect on TNFα release from these cells, whereas GW, an inhibitor of both ADAM10 and ADAM17, further reduced TNFα release (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: TNFα expression by LPS is normal in FRMD8 knockout iPSC-derived macrophages.
source: Although shedding was inhibited, TNFα expression by LPS was normal in these cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mature ADAM17 levels are reduced in all tissues examined from Frmd8-/- mice compared to wild-type littermates.
source: Western blot analysis of tissues of Frmd8-/- mice showed that mature ADAM17 levels were reduced in all tissues examined compared to tissues from wild-type littermates (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: There is a major reduction of mature ADAM17 levels in the brain of Frmd8-/- mice, a tissue in which iRhom2 is almost completely absent but iRhom1 levels are high.
source: Of note, there was a major reduction of mature ADAM17 levels in the brain, a tissue in which iRhom2 in almost completely absent but iRhom1 levels are high (Christova et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015). This supports our hypothesis that FRMD8 regulates mature ADAM17 levels through iRhom1 as well as iRhom2.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9D and previous literature (Christova et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).

claim: In lung and skin of Frmd8-/- mice, there is a strong decrease of iRhom2 protein levels compared to wild-type.
source: In lung and skin, both tissues with high iRhom2 expression (Christova et al., 2013), we detected a strong decrease of iRhom2 protein levels in Frmd8-/- compared to wild-type (Figure 9E, Figure 9—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9E and Figure 9—figure supplement 2C, and previous literature (Christova et al., 2013).

claim: The reduction of endogenous iRhom2 and mature ADAM17 levels in mouse lung is about 75%.
source: The reduction of endogenous iRhom2 and mature ADAM17 levels in mouse lung was about 75% (Figure 9E), which is comparable to the reduction of mature ADAM17 levels in iPSC-derived human macrophages (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by western blot quantification data shown in Figure 9E and 9B.

claim: Frmd8-/- mice are viable and fertile.
source: Frmd8-/- mice are viable (Figure 9—figure supplement 2B) and fertile.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by breeding data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2B.

claim: FRMD8 acts to prevent the endolysosomal degradation of the iRhom/ADAM17 complex.
source: Despite this long-term relationship, we have found no evidence for a functional role for FRMD8 in ER-to-Golgi trafficking or ADAM17 maturation. Instead, FRMD8 acts later, to prevent the endolysosomal degradation of the iRhom/ADAM17 complex (Figure 10).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the data showing lysosomal accumulation in the absence of FRMD8 (Figure 6) and rescue by lysosomal inhibitors (Figure 6G).

claim: It would be more appropriate to consider ADAM17 as the active subunit of a regulatory complex at the cell surface, where iRhoms provide regulatory functions and FRMD8 maintains the stability of the iRhom/ADAM17 complex post-ADAM17 maturation.
source: Combined with our previous studies (Grieve et al., 2017), this work has changed our perspective on ADAM17, the central enzyme in cytokine and growth factor shedding. Our evidence implies that it would be more appropriate to consider it as the active subunit of a regulatory complex at the cell surface, where iRhoms provide regulatory functions (Maney et al., 2015; Cavadas et al., 2017; Grieve et al., 2017), and FRMD8 maintains the stability of the iRhom/ADAM17 complex post-ADAM17 maturation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the data presented in this study and previous literature (Grieve et al., 2017; Maney et al., 2015; Cavadas et al., 2017).

claim: FRMD8 binds to the cytoplasmic tail of LRP6 co-receptor, preventing the recruitment of axin and negatively regulating Wnt signalling.
source: In the only other paper about FRMD8 function, it was reported that FRMD8 (named Bili, after the Drosophila mutation) negatively regulates Wnt signalling by binding to the LRP6 co-receptor, thereby preventing the recruitment of the signal transduction protein axin (Kategaya et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by previous literature (Kategaya et al., 2009).

claim: The cub mutation is described as a gain-of-function mutation that leads to constitutively elevated release of amphiregulin, but is also reported to be defective in releasing TNFα.
source: cub was described as a gain-of-function mutation that leads to constitutively elevated release of amphiregulin, but is also reported to be defective in releasing TNFα (Hosur et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by previous literature (Hosur et al., 2014).

claim: Specific point mutations in the N-terminus of human iRhom2 are the cause of tylosis with oesophageal cancer (TOC).
source: Second, specific point mutations in the N-terminus of human iRhom2 are the cause of a rare genetic disorder called tylosis with oesophageal cancer (TOC) (Blaydon et al., 2012; Saarinen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by previous literature (Blaydon et al., 2012; Saarinen et al., 2012).

claim: TOC mutations and truncation of parts of the iRhom2 N-terminus have been reported to enhance the activity of ADAM17.
source: TOC mutations, as well as truncation of parts of the N-terminus have been reported to enhance the activity of ADAM17 (Maney et al., 2015), leading to the conclusion that parts of the N-terminus have inhibitory functions on ADAM17 function.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by previous literature (Maney et al., 2015).

claim: Phosphorylation of specific sites in the iRhom2 N-terminus results in 14-3-3 binding and consequent activation of substrate shedding by associated ADAM17.
source: Third, phosphorylation of specific sites in the iRhom2 N-terminus result in 14-3-3 binding and consequent activation of substrate shedding by associated ADAM17 (Grieve et al., 2017; Cavadas et al., 2017), demonstrating that the N-terminus of iRhom2 also positively regulates ADAM17.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by previous literature (Grieve et al., 2017; Cavadas et al., 2017).

claim: The FRMD8 binding region does not overlap with sites required for phosphorylation-dependent 14-3-3 binding.
source: The FRMD8 binding region does not overlap with these sites required for phosphorylation-dependent 14-3-3 binding, however it is formally possible that there is some functional overlap between them.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the mapping data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Major changes in the interaction of FRMD8 with iRhom2 upon PMA stimulation could not be detected.
source: We could not detect major changes in the interaction of FRMD8 with iRhom2 upon PMA stimulation (Figure 10—figure supplement 1), which leads to the phosphorylation of iRhoms (Grieve et al., 2017; Cavadas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1 and previous literature (Grieve et al., 2017; Cavadas et al., 2017).

claim: An iRhom2 mutant in which 15 conserved phosphorylation sites have been mutated to alanine (iRhom2pDEAD) does not abolish the interaction with FRMD8.
source: Moreover, an iRhom2 mutant, in which 15 conserved phosphorylation sites have been mutated to alanine (iRhom2pDEAD; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) (Grieve et al., 2017), did not abolish the interaction with FRMD8 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1). This conclusively demonstrates that the binding of FRMD8 to iRhom2 does not require phosphorylation of iRhom2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1 and previous literature (Grieve et al., 2017).

claim: iRhom2 lacking the entire N-terminus is not sufficient to support ADAM17-mediated shedding in iRhom1/2-deficient cells, although it can promote ER-to-Golgi trafficking of ADAM17.
source: Consistent with our current results, we reported previously that iRhom2 lacking the entire N-terminus is not sufficient to support ADAM17-mediated shedding in iRhom1/2-deficient cells, although it can promote ER-to-Golgi trafficking of ADAM17 (Grieve et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by previous literature (Grieve et al., 2017).

claim: iRhom2 knockout mice are broadly healthy, beyond defects in TNFα and type I interferon signalling that are only apparent upon challenge by bacterial and viral infections.
source: iRhom2 knockout mice are broadly healthy, beyond defects in TNFα and type I interferon signalling that are only apparent upon challenge by bacterial and viral infections (McIlwain et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by previous literature (McIlwain et al., 2012; Luo et al., 2016).

claim: Even in cells with complete loss of FRMD8, there is still a low level of mature ADAM17 at the cell surface and consequently residual TNFα shedding.
source: This is supported, at least in principle, by our observation that even in cells with complete loss of FRMD8, there is still a low level of mature ADAM17 at the cell surface, and consequently residual TNFα shedding.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the data shown in Figures 2 and 9.

claim: Mice with a hypomorphic mutation in ADAM17 (termed ADAM17ex/ex) show that even only 5% of normal ADAM17 expression is sufficient to rescue many aspects of the loss of function phenotype.
source: Consistent with this idea, mice with a hypomorphic mutation in ADAM17 (termed ADAM17ex/ex) show that even only 5% of normal ADAM17 expression is sufficient to rescue many aspects of the loss of function phenotype (Chalaris et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by previous literature (Chalaris et al., 2010).

claim: Reduced levels of ADAM17 in the Adam17ex/ex mouse limits colorectal cancer formation and any residual tumours are low-grade dysplasias.
source: Moreover, a recent study has shown that reducing ADAM17 levels has great pharmaceutical potential: reduced levels of ADAM17 in the Adam17ex/ex mouse limits colorectal cancer formation and any residual tumours are low-grade dysplasias (Schmidt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by previous literature (Schmidt et al., 2018).

claim: ADAM17 is also called TACE.
source: The cell surface protease ADAM17 (also called TACE) mediates the release of many important signalling molecules by 'shedding' their extracellular ligand domains from transmembrane precursors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: TNFα is a primary cytokine involved in the inflammatory responses to infection and tissue damage.
source: A prominent example is the role of ADAM17 in releasing tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) (Black et al., 1997; Moss et al., 1997), a primary cytokine involved in the inflammatory responses to infection and tissue damage (Kalliolias and Ivashkiv, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Kalliolias and Ivashkiv, 2016).

claim: ADAM17 is the principal sheddase of the epidermal growth factor (EGF) receptor ligands amphiregulin (AREG), transforming growth factor alpha (TGFα), heparin-binding EGF (HB-EGF), epigen, and epiregulin.
source: In addition, ADAM17 is the principal sheddase of the epidermal growth factor (EGF) receptor ligands amphiregulin (AREG), transforming growth factor alpha (TGFα), heparin-binding EGF (HB-EGF), epigen, and epiregulin (Sahin et al., 2004; Sahin and Blobel, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Sahin et al., 2004; Sahin and Blobel, 2007).

claim: iRhoms can effectively be considered as regulatory subunits of ADAM17.
source: We and others have previously reported that the rhomboid-like iRhom proteins have a specific and extensive regulatory relationship with ADAM17, to the extent that iRhoms can effectively be considered as regulatory subunits of the protease (Grieve et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Grieve et al., 2017).

claim: iRhoms are members of the rhomboid-like superfamily.
source: iRhoms are members of a wider family of evolutionarily related multi-pass membrane proteins, called the rhomboid-like superfamily (Freeman, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Freeman, 2014).

claim: The rhomboid-like superfamily is named after the rhomboids, intramembrane serine proteases that cleave substrate transmembrane domains (TMDs).
source: The family is named after the rhomboids, intramembrane serine proteases that cleave substrate transmembrane domains (TMDs), but many members, including iRhoms, have lost protease activity during evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: Many members of the rhomboid-like superfamily, including iRhoms, have lost protease activity during evolution.
source: The family is named after the rhomboids, intramembrane serine proteases that cleave substrate transmembrane domains (TMDs), but many members, including iRhoms, have lost protease activity during evolution.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: iRhom1 and iRhom2 show redundancy in regulating ADAM17 maturation, but differ in their tissue expression.
source: iRhom1 and its paralogue iRhom2 (encoded by the genes RHBDF1 and RHBDF2) show redundancy in regulating ADAM17 maturation, but differ in their tissue expression (Christova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Christova et al., 2013).

claim: Many cell types express both iRhoms, so the loss of one can be compensated by the other.
source: Many cell types express both iRhoms, so the loss of one can be compensated by the other (Christova et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Christova et al., 2013; Li et al., 2015).

claim: Macrophages do not express iRhom1, so iRhom2 alone regulates ADAM17 and therefore TNFα inflammatory signalling in macrophages.
source: Macrophages are, however, an exception: iRhom1 is not expressed, so iRhom2 alone regulates ADAM17 and therefore TNFα inflammatory signalling in macrophages (Adrain et al., 2012; McIlwain et al., 2012; Issuree et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Adrain et al., 2012; McIlwain et al., 2012; Issuree et al., 2013).

claim: iRhoms bind to the catalytically immature pro-form of ADAM17 (proADAM17) in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and are required for its trafficking from the ER to the Golgi apparatus.
source: First, they bind to the catalytically immature pro-form of ADAM17 (proADAM17) in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and are required for its trafficking from the ER to the Golgi apparatus (Adrain et al., 2012; McIlwain et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Adrain et al., 2012; McIlwain et al., 2012).

claim: Once proADAM17 reaches the Golgi, it is matured by the removal of its inhibitory pro-domain by pro-protein convertases.
source: Once proADAM17 reaches the Golgi, it is matured by the removal of its inhibitory pro-domain by pro-protein convertases (Schlöndorff et al., 2000; Endres et al., 2003) and is further trafficked to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Schlöndorff et al., 2000; Endres et al., 2003).

claim: iRhom2 prevents the lysosomal degradation of ADAM17.
source: Still bound to each other, iRhom2 prevents the lysosomal degradation of ADAM17 (Grieve et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Grieve et al., 2017).

claim: The phosphorylation of the iRhom2 cytoplasmic tail promotes the recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins, which promote the shedding activity of ADAM17.
source: Later, iRhom2 controls the activation of ADAM17: the phosphorylation of the iRhom2 cytoplasmic tail promotes the recruitment of 14-3-3 proteins, which promote the shedding activity of ADAM17, thereby releasing TNFα from the cell surface in response to inflammatory triggers (Grieve et al., 2017; Cavadas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Grieve et al., 2017; Cavadas et al., 2017).

claim: iRhoms are reported to contribute to ADAM17 substrate specificity.
source: Finally, iRhoms are also reported to contribute to ADAM17 substrate specificity (Maretzky et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Maretzky et al., 2013).

claim: Anti-TNFα therapies, used to treat rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, are currently the biggest grossing drugs in the world.
source: The significance of this potential is underlined by the fact that anti-TNFα therapies, used to treat rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, are currently the biggest grossing drugs in the world (Monaco et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by previous literature (Monaco et al., 2015).
